characters: Mansa: a determined Ghanaian girl introduced at age fourteen in JHS 2 in the Bono Region and later shown as a twenty-four-year-old food-science entrepreneur wearing a clean white hairnet, green polo shirt and lab coat.
Mensah: Mansa’s cousin and co-founder, an operations and accounting mind wearing spectacles and a yellow-and-green collared shirt.
Auntie Yaa: a hardworking plantain and cassava farmer in her forties, wearing a bright green wax-print cloth and head-wrap.
Mr Ofori: an inspector and food-safety advisor from the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA Ghana), wearing a white inspection coat and carrying a moisture meter.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, confident Ghanaian narrator (en-GH); articulate and determined for Mansa and Mensah, warm for Auntie Yaa, professional for Mr Ofori.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 125 words per minute); pause clearly around the batch cost and margin numbers on pages 8–9.
notes: Pronounce Mansa ("MAHN-sah"), Yaa ("YAAH") and Ofori ("oh-FOH-ree") clearly.

music: Optional upbeat acoustic guitar and light percussion; off by default.
culturalNotes: Highlights Bono Region agriculture (Sunyani) and the link between smallholder women farmers and youth-led agro-processing.
reviewQuestions: Are the unit economics (200 + 150 = 350 cost; 500 revenue; 150 profit = 30% margin) and FDA/GSA standards clear and accurate?

pages.brief: Sunny Bono Region roadside market: Mansa (14, green school uniform) and Mensah (14, spectacles) standing with farmer Auntie Yaa (green wax-print dress) beside baskets of ripe yellow plantains and cassava tubers.
pages.narration: Set up the economic paradox clearly: post-harvest gluts on farms alongside expensive imported snacks in shops.

pages.brief: JHS Career Technology classroom: the teacher showing Mansa and Mensah a fresh bunch of plantains beside sealed jars of golden plantain crisps and fine white cassava flour (no text labels).
pages.narration: Clear food-science explanation of moisture removal, shelf life and value addition.

pages.brief: Clean starter food-processing room in Sunyani: Mansa (now 24, white hairnet, green polo, white food-coat) and Mensah (spectacles, notebook) inspecting a stainless-steel slicing table with Auntie Yaa.
pages.narration: Show realistic preparation: years of study in food science and accounting before launching.

pages.brief: Small office desk: Mensah pointing to a steep red interest chart vs a manageable green step-by-step lease plan on his laptop (no text) while Mansa nods in agreement.
pages.narration: Realistic financial lesson: why high-interest debt can sink a young manufacturing business and how disciplined financing works.

pages.brief: Inside the processing workshop: Mansa in hairnet and gloves working beside a Ghanaian technician to fit a silver circulation fan and temperature dial onto a stainless-steel food dehydrator.
pages.narration: Show technical persistence and refusal to sell substandard products.

pages.brief: Spotless food-processing room: Mr Ofori (white inspection coat, moisture meter) testing a bowl of fine flour while Mansa and Mensah in hairnets and aprons stand beside a stainless-steel handwashing sink.
pages.narration: Highlight Ghana’s real regulatory standards: FDA Ghana food safety registration and GSA quality standards.

pages.brief: Mansa holding up a framed official certificate with a green seal (no text) beside rows of neatly sealed golden-and-green snack pouches on a stainless-steel counter.
pages.narration: Strong business ethics: food safety and regulatory integrity are non-negotiable.

pages.brief: At the workshop planning board: Mensah pointing to two visual cost stacks, two green coin stacks by a basket of plantains and one-and-a-half gold coin stacks by sealed pouches (no text or numbers).
pages.narration: Walk through the exact cost arithmetic clearly: 200 + 150 = 350 cedis for 100 packs (3.50 cedis per pack).

pages.brief: Clean packing area: uniformed young workers packing sealed green-and-gold plantain crisp pouches into neat cardboard cartons while Mansa and Mensah check the inventory sheet.
pages.narration: Clear profit and margin arithmetic: 100 × 5 = 500 cedis revenue; 500 − 350 = 150 cedis profit (30% of 500).

pages.brief: Bright modern Ghanaian supermarket aisle: Mansa in a branded green apron offering sample cups of golden plantain crisps to smiling Ghanaian families beside a prominent display shelf (no readable text).
pages.narration: Show how quality, packaging and reliability win customers fairly in a competitive market.

pages.brief: Sunny courtyard of a clean modern Ghanaian agro-processing plant with solar panels on the roof: Mansa, Mensah and Auntie Yaa smiling with eighteen uniformed factory staff and farmers beside a delivery van.
pages.narration: Measurable, realistic 4-year impact: 18 factory jobs + 45 contracted smallholder farmers and reduced post-harvest loss.

pages.brief: Through a large glass viewing corridor in the clean food plant: Mansa and Mensah showing JHS students in visitor coats how golden plantains are sliced, dried and sealed inside the gleaming workshop.
pages.narration: Inspiring, grounded finale celebrating Ghanaian agro-industrial pride.

teacherGuide.overview: A rich JHS 1–3 entrepreneurship, food-science and career-technology story showing how Ghanaian agro-processing turns perishable farm gluts into shelf-stable products. It covers moisture control, financing challenges (avoiding predatory interest rates), engineering troubleshooting, compliance with the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA Ghana) and Ghana Standards Authority (GSA), unit-cost and profit-margin arithmetic, and multi-year job creation.
learningGoals: Explain how agro-processing (moisture reduction, hygienic packaging) prevents post-harvest loss and adds economic value to Ghanaian crops.
Describe the regulatory roles of the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA Ghana) and the Ghana Standards Authority (GSA) in protecting consumers.
Calculate batch cost, revenue, gross profit and percentage margin (200 + 150 = 350 cedis cost; 100 × 5 = 500 cedis revenue; 500 − 350 = 150 cedis profit = 30% margin).
Recognise that sustainable enterprises require skills, ethical compliance, financing discipline and years of persistence.
beforeReading: Preview the title and cover illustration with learners and ask what real-world problem or question the characters might face.
whileReading: Pause at the embedded comprehension and vocabulary activities to check understanding and discuss the evidence in the text.
afterReading: Value-Addition Price Check: Compare the price per kilogram of raw cassava or plantain in the local market with the price per kilogram of packaged gari, plantain crisps or fufu flour, and list all the processing and packaging steps that account for the added value.

Batch Margin Worksheet: Calculate unit cost, revenue, profit and margin for 200 packs of gari if raw cassava costs 300 cedis, roasting/packaging costs 200 cedis, and each pack sells for 4 cedis (Cost = 500; Revenue = 800; Profit = 300; Margin = 37.5%).
discussion: Why do raw cassava tubers and ripe plantains spoil rapidly if they are not processed or cooled?
Why did Mensah turn down the 28% bank loan in their second month and choose a phased equipment lease instead?
When 20 batches scorched in the uneven dryer, or when a distributor suggested printing a fake FDA number, what choices showed Mansa and Mensah’s integrity?
How did the factory benefit both the 18 full-time workers in town and the 45 smallholder farmers in Auntie Yaa’s cooperative?
reflection: How did the factory benefit both the 18 full-time workers in town and the 45 smallholder farmers in Auntie Yaa’s cooperative?

whatWeKnow: Reducing water activity (moisture content below ~12% in flours and dried crisps) inhibits microbial growth and enzymatic spoilage, extending shelf life from days to months.

In Ghana, the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA, under the Public Health Act, 2012, Act 851) regulates food safety and product registration, while the Ghana Standards Authority (GSA) sets national quality and metrology standards.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Ghanaian food scientists are developing vitamin-enriched composite flours blending local cassava, orange-fleshed sweet potato and soybean to reduce wheat imports and improve child nutrition.

investigation.title: Safe Sun-Drying Moisture Loss Observation
materials: One fresh slice of plantain or apple, a small clean plate, a fine mesh cover (to keep flies away), and a kitchen scale (or ruler to measure thickness).
steps: Measure the starting mass (or thickness in millimetres) of a thin slice of fresh plantain on a clean plate covered with clean mesh.
Place the covered plate in warm sunshine for 4 hours, then measure the mass (or thickness) again.
Observe how the slice becomes lighter, firmer and drier as water evaporates, the exact principle behind food dehydration!

pronunciation.guidance: a single long "YAAH" (the double a marks a long vowel).
reviewerNotes: Confirm vowel length; engines may shorten it to "ya".
